name: Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death

clinicalPearls: Harrison distinguishes three overlapping terms: cardiovascular collapse is sudden loss of effective circulation that may revert spontaneously (e.g., neurocardiogenic syncope) or require intervention; cardiac arrest is abrupt cessation of cardiac function with loss of circulation potentially reversible by prompt intervention; and sudden cardiac death is unexpected death from cardiac arrest occurring within roughly 1 hour of symptom onset (p.2332-2333).

Sudden cardiac death accounts for about 15% of all deaths and roughly half of all cardiac deaths; in the United States the text cites an estimated 350,000 EMS-attended out-of-hospital arrests and 210,000 sudden cardiac deaths in adults yearly (p.2332).

Up to two-thirds of sudden cardiac deaths occur as the first clinical manifestation of previously undiagnosed heart disease, limiting the ability to predict and prevent events at the population level (p.2332).

Coronary heart disease underlies the majority of sudden cardiac deaths, but the proportion attributable to coronary disease varies markedly by demographics: roughly 70% in white men versus 40-50% in women and black individuals, and under 40% in Asian populations (p.2333-2334).

The text emphasizes the chain of survival for out-of-hospital arrest, and that survival is strongly time-dependent: neurologic recovery falls rapidly and is under 30% by 5 minutes from collapse to return of spontaneous circulation when no bystander CPR is given (p.2335-2338).

Gasping (agonal) respirations and brief seizure-like activity are common during arrest and may be misinterpreted as breathing or responsiveness, leading to delayed resuscitation; a pulse check by a trained provider should take no longer than 10 seconds (p.2335-2336).

The initial recorded rhythm carries prognostic and etiologic weight: ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation (shockable rhythms) have the best outcomes, while pulseless electrical activity and asystole carry a poor prognosis (p.2335-2336).

The proportion of arrests found in ventricular fibrillation has fallen from over half in the 1970s to only 20-25% in recent series, with pulseless electrical activity and asystole now most common; because arrhythmias are unstable after collapse, the rhythm at EMS arrival may not reflect the initiating rhythm (p.2334).

Inherited arrhythmia syndromes without structural heart disease (long QT, Brugada, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, early repolarization, idiopathic VF) are a more important cause of sudden death in the young and in Asian populations, accounting for around 10% of cases in Asia versus 1-2% in Western countries (p.2334).

Depressed left ventricular function is the best-validated risk marker in structural heart disease; after myocardial infarction, SCD risk rises gradually as LVEF falls toward 40% and then increases exponentially below that (p.2338-2339).

Following an MI, the risk of sudden death rises up to roughly 10-fold, with the highest absolute rates in the first 30 days; early deaths are more often non-arrhythmic (myocardial rupture, reinfarction) while later deaths are predominantly scar-related ventricular arrhythmias (p.2334-2335).

Commotio cordis - ventricular fibrillation triggered by blunt, non-penetrating precordial impact - is a rare cause of sudden death in otherwise healthy individuals, especially after a chest blow during the vulnerable repolarization window (p.2335).
harrison.pathophysiology: Most sudden cardiac death stems from a lethal ventricular tachyarrhythmia (polymorphic VT degenerating to ventricular fibrillation) arising on a vulnerable myocardial substrate, though bradyarrhythmia, asystole, and pulseless electrical activity are increasingly common terminal rhythms. Coronary artery disease is the predominant substrate, acting through acute ischemia/infarction or through reentry around scar from a healed infarct. Nonischemic processes - dilated, hypertrophic, infiltrative, and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathies, valvular disease, congenital surgical scars, and myocarditis - produce replacement fibrosis, hypertrophy, ventricular stretch, electrical heterogeneity, altered ion-channel function, and abnormal calcium handling that lower the threshold for sustained arrhythmia. In structurally normal hearts, inherited channelopathies (long QT, Brugada, CPVT), pre-excited atrial fibrillation in Wolff-Parkinson-White, and QT-prolonging drug toxicity cause primary electrical arrest. Pulseless electrical activity reflects mechanical or metabolic catastrophe - massive MI, pulmonary embolism, exsanguination, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, profound hypoxia or acidosis. Heightened autonomic (sympathetic) tone is the common thread linking precipitants such as vigorous exertion, emotional and environmental stress to arrhythmogenesis. After return of circulation, global ischemia-reperfusion brain injury becomes the dominant determinant of outcome.
additionalDifferentials: Vasovagal/neurocardiogenic syncope (transient, self-limited circulatory loss rather than true arrest)
Profound metabolic derangement (severe hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, severe hypokalemia)
Drug overdose (including opioid and QT-prolonging agents)
Primary respiratory arrest with secondary circulatory collapse
infectionMimics: Myocarditis presenting with malignant ventricular arrhythmia
additionalInvestigations: Continuous ECG/rhythm monitoring and retrieval of AED rhythm strips to determine the initiating rhythm
Arterial blood gas to assess hypoxia and metabolic acidosis during and after resuscitation
Serum electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) and assessment for reversible causes
Post-ROSC 12-lead ECG to detect ST-elevation MI and consideration of coronary angiography
Echocardiography to assess LVEF, prior infarction, valvular and structural disease
Cardiac MRI to characterize scar burden/heterogeneity and nonischemic cardiomyopathy
Cardiac PET and/or endomyocardial biopsy when inflammatory cardiomyopathy (sarcoidosis, myocarditis) is suspected
Electrophysiology study and provocative testing (epinephrine challenge for LQTS, sodium-channel-blocker challenge for Brugada) and genetic evaluation when a heritable arrhythmia syndrome is suspected
EEG monitoring in comatose post-arrest patients to detect seizures and prognosticate
redFlags: Unresponsiveness with absent or only agonal/gasping respirations
Absent central pulse on a brief (<=10 second) check
Pulseless electrical activity or asystole as the presenting rhythm (poor prognosis)
Long interval (>5 minutes) between collapse and start of resuscitation
Hemodynamic instability, recurrent VT/VF, or signs of ongoing ischemia after ROSC
Post-ROSC absent pupillary light reflex, status myoclonus, absent EEG reactivity, or persistent burst suppression (predict poor neurologic recovery)
Sustained monomorphic VT or VF without a clearly reversible cause, implying high recurrence risk
Markedly depressed LVEF (e.g., <=35%) or clinical heart failure after MI
harrison.prognosis: Outcomes are dominated by time to resuscitation and the presenting rhythm. Survival to hospital discharge for out-of-hospital arrest has improved but remains low - the chapter states about 90% of patients do not survive to discharge, and roughly 20% of survivors are left with severe neurologic or physical disability. Shockable rhythms (VT/VF) carry the best prognosis, with survival approaching 30% in some regions, whereas PEA and asystole carry poor outcomes. Success of resuscitation declines sharply after 5 minutes from collapse. Ischemia-reperfusion brain injury accounts for over two-thirds of post-arrest deaths; reliable neurologic prognostication is generally deferred at least 72 hours after return to normothermia (typically 4-5 days post-arrest). Features predicting poor neurologic outcome include absent pupillary light reflex, status myoclonus, absent EEG reactivity, and persistent burst suppression.
pitfalls: Mistaking agonal gasping or brief seizure activity for effective breathing or responsiveness, delaying CPR
Spending more than 10 seconds on a pulse check and thereby delaying chest compressions
Assuming the rhythm at EMS arrival reflects the initiating rhythm, when VF and bradyarrhythmias commonly degenerate to asystole
Prognosticating neurologic recovery too early - while still under sedation/hypothermia or before the recommended 72 hours of normothermia
Implanting an ICD for arrhythmia driven by a transient reversible cause (e.g., hyperkalemia, drug-induced torsades, or VF within 48 h of acute MI), where it is generally not indicated
Withholding consideration that arrhythmia may signal end-stage heart disease, in which an ICD will not change the course absent transplant or assist-device candidacy
Overlooking treatable PEA/asystole causes such as pulmonary embolism, hypovolemia, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, hypoxia, acidosis, hyperkalemia, hypothermia, toxins, and massive MI
Attributing sudden death in the young to coronary disease, when HCM, coronary anomalies, myocarditis, ARVC, and channelopathies are more often responsible
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison frames the spectrum by terminology and reversibility: cardiovascular collapse (may revert spontaneously, includes syncope) -> cardiac arrest (rarely reverts spontaneously; reversibility depends on mechanism, setting, and speed of intervention) -> sudden cardiac death (death within ~1 hour of symptom onset). Acute risk and outcome stratify by presenting rhythm - shockable (VT/VF, better) versus non-shockable (PEA/asystole, worse). Chronic SCD risk in structural heart disease is graded chiefly by LVEF and presence of heart failure, with risk rising gradually as LVEF falls to 40% and exponentially below it.
management: Initiate the chain of survival immediately with high-quality chest compressions and early defibrillation for shockable rhythms
Deliver advanced life support with adrenaline and rapid identification and correction of reversible causes
After return of spontaneous circulation, provide targeted temperature management and post-resuscitation intensive care
Obtain an urgent post-resuscitation ECG and proceed to coronary angiography and revascularisation where acute coronary occlusion is suspected
Correct electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia and treat the underlying arrhythmic substrate
Implant a cardioverter-defibrillator for secondary prevention in survivors with an ongoing arrhythmic substrate
Screen relatives and offer genetic counselling where an inherited arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy is identified
